title: REG U1·W3 — Individual Taxation II: Deductions, QBI, Credits & Computation (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — from AGI to the check

Last week ended at AGI. This week finishes the individual return: subtract the greater of the standard or itemized deduction and the qualified business income (QBI) deduction to reach taxable income, apply the rate schedule (with preferential rates on qualified dividends and long-term gains), and subtract credits to reach the liability — then compare to payments. The QBI deduction in particular matters to MBG's owner, because a construction contractor is not a specified service business.

Standard versus itemized deductions

A taxpayer deducts the greater of the standard deduction (a fixed amount by filing status, larger for the age-65-or-blind) or itemized deductions on Schedule A. After the TCJA nearly doubled the standard deduction, most taxpayers take it, so the exam tests when itemizing wins.

Itemized deductions (Schedule A)

The main itemized categories: medical expenses to the extent they exceed 7.5% of AGI; state and local taxes (SALT) — income (or sales) plus property taxes — capped at $10,000 ($5,000 MFS); home mortgage interest on acquisition debt up to $750,000 (post-TCJA; older loans grandfathered at $1,000,000); investment interest limited to net investment income; charitable contributions — cash up to 60% of AGI, and appreciated long-term capital-gain property at fair market value up to 30% of AGI; and casualty and theft losses only if attributable to a federally declared disaster. Miscellaneous 2%-of-AGI itemized deductions are suspended through 2025.

The qualified business income deduction (§199A)

Owners of passthrough businesses (sole proprietorships, partnerships, S corporations) may deduct up to 20% of qualified business income — a deduction taken after AGI that does not reduce SE tax. The deduction is the lesser of (a) 20% of QBI or (b) 20% of taxable income minus net capital gain (net capital gain includes qualified dividends). Above taxable-income thresholds, two further limits apply: a W-2 wages / UBIA-of-property cap, and a phaseout for a specified service trade or business (SSTB) — law, accounting, health, consulting, and similar. Construction is not an SSTB, so MBG's owner keeps the deduction even above the threshold (subject only to the wage/property cap). Worked limit: if QBI is $100,000 and taxable income less net capital gain is $90,000, the deduction is the lesser of $20,000 (20% × QBI) or $18,000 (20% × $90,000) = $18,000 — the taxable-income limit binds.

Computing the tax

Ordinary taxable income runs through the progressive rate brackets for the filing status. But qualified dividends and net long-term capital gains are pulled out and taxed at the preferential 0% / 15% / 20% rates, stacked on top of ordinary income to determine which preferential rate applies. High earners also owe the 3.8% net investment income tax on the lesser of net investment income or the excess of modified AGI over a threshold. The result is the gross tax before credits.

Credits — nonrefundable and refundable

Credits reduce tax dollar-for-dollar and are more valuable than deductions. Nonrefundable credits can reduce the tax to zero but not below: the base child tax credit, the child and dependent care credit, the lifetime learning education credit, the foreign tax credit, and the retirement savings credit. Refundable credits can generate a refund beyond the tax owed: the earned income credit (EIC), the additional child tax credit, and the partly refundable American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC). Knowing which credits are refundable is a recurring exam point.

The alternative minimum tax

The AMT is a parallel system that limits the benefit of certain preferences. Start from regular taxable income, add back preference and adjustment items (the SALT deduction, certain depreciation, private-activity-bond interest, incentive-stock-option bargain elements), subtract the AMT exemption (phased out at higher income), and apply the 26%/28% AMT rates to alternative minimum taxable income. The taxpayer pays the greater of regular tax or the tentative minimum tax. Because the TCJA raised the exemption, far fewer individuals owe AMT now, but it remains testable.

Payments and the construction owner

The liability is settled by withholding (from wages) and quarterly estimated payments. A self-employed contractor like MBG's owner has no withholding, so estimates matter: to avoid an underpayment penalty the taxpayer generally must pay the lesser of 90% of the current-year tax or 100% of the prior-year tax (110% if prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000). Putting it together — deductions, the QBI deduction, the rate schedule, credits, and payments — converts the AGI from last week into the final number on the return, and completes the individual-tax arc of REG Unit 1.

Education and family credits in detail

The exam tests the contours of the common credits. The American Opportunity Tax Credit is up to $2,500 per student (100% of the first $2,000 of qualified expenses plus 25% of the next $2,000) for the first four years of postsecondary education, and is 40% refundable. The Lifetime Learning Credit is 20% of up to $10,000 of expenses (a $2,000 maximum) per return, nonrefundable, with no year limit. The child tax credit is a per-qualifying-child amount that phases out at higher AGI, with a refundable additional child tax credit portion. The child and dependent care credit is a percentage of up to $3,000 of care expenses for one dependent ($6,000 for two or more) incurred to enable the taxpayer to work. Each credit has its own AGI phaseout, which is why they are sequenced carefully on the return.

Additional taxes and the underpayment mechanics

Beyond the income tax and AMT, high earners face the 0.9% additional Medicare tax on wages and self-employment income above a threshold and the 3.8% net investment income tax on the lesser of net investment income or modified AGI over the threshold. The return reconciles the total tax to payments — withholding (treated as paid evenly through the year) plus quarterly estimates. If payments fall short of the safe harbor, the §6654 underpayment penalty accrues like interest on the shortfall for each quarter it persists. Because a contractor's income is lumpy, the annualized-income installment method can lower the required payment in slow quarters, matching estimates to when the construction cash actually arrives rather than assuming even income.

CMA bridge

CMA month 9 weighed decisions on a marginal, after-tax basis; REG supplies the actual individual-tax machinery behind that after-tax rate — the brackets, the preferential rates on capital gains, the QBI deduction, and the credits that determine an owner's true marginal cost of a dollar of construction profit.

Practice and recap

  1. Take the greater of the standard or itemized deduction; know the SALT $10,000 cap, the 7.5%-of-AGI medical floor, and the $750,000 mortgage-acquisition limit.
  2. Apply §199A: 20% of QBI, limited to 20% of taxable income less net capital gain; construction is not an SSTB.
  3. Tax ordinary income at the brackets; tax qualified dividends and LTCG at 0/15/20%.
  4. Separate refundable credits (EIC, additional CTC, AOTC) from nonrefundable; pay estimates at 90%/100%/110% safe harbors.

Recap: taxable income is AGI minus the greater of standard or itemized deductions and minus the §199A QBI deduction (lesser of 20% of QBI or 20% of taxable income less net capital gain); ordinary income runs the brackets while qualified dividends and long-term gains get 0/15/20%; refundable credits like the EIC can exceed the tax; and a self-employed owner avoids penalty by meeting the 90%/100%/110% estimated-tax safe harbor.

flashcards.back: Deduct the greater of the two; itemized deductions go on Schedule A.
$10,000 ($5,000 MFS) for combined state/local income (or sales) and property taxes.
Interest on acquisition debt up to $750,000 (older loans grandfathered at $1,000,000).
Deductible only to the extent total medical expenses exceed 7.5% of AGI.
Cash up to 60% of AGI; appreciated long-term capital-gain property at FMV up to 30% of AGI.
Lesser of 20% of QBI or 20% of (taxable income − net capital gain); W-2/UBIA cap + SSTB phaseout above thresholds. Construction is not an SSTB.
Refundable (EIC, additional CTC, partial AOTC) can produce a refund; nonrefundable (base CTC, child-care, LLC, foreign tax) only reduce tax to zero.
Qualified dividends and net long-term capital gains are taxed at 0%/15%/20%.

quiz.title: Individual Taxation II — Deductions, QBI & Credits

questions.q: The itemized deduction for state and local taxes (SALT) is capped at:
The §199A qualified business income deduction is generally:
choices: 20% of qualified business income, subject to taxable-income and wage limits
A credit equal to self-employment tax
questions.explain: §199A allows up to 20% of QBI from passthroughs, limited to 20% of taxable income less net capital gain (plus wage/SSTB limits above thresholds).

choices: Can reduce the tax to zero but not below
questions.explain: Nonrefundable credits can offset tax only down to zero; refundable credits can generate a refund.

questions.q: Qualified dividends and net long-term capital gains are taxed at:
questions.explain: They receive the preferential 0%, 15%, or 20% rates depending on income.

questions.q: Itemized medical expenses are deductible only to the extent they exceed:
questions.explain: Only medical expenses above 7.5% of AGI are deductible.
The EIC is refundable; the others listed are nonrefundable.

questions.q: Which business is NOT a specified service trade or business, so its owner can claim QBI even above the threshold (subject to the wage/property cap)?
questions.explain: Construction is not an SSTB; law, accounting, and consulting are SSTBs subject to the QBI phaseout above the thresholds.
